newsitem.title: USA: NASD vp sees key changes in market enforcement.
newsitem.headline: NASD vp sees key changes in market enforcement.

text.p: The National Association of Securities Dealers's new enforcement chief told bond dealers on Friday to get ready for major changes in the way NASD enforces its rules in the wake of this year's SEC settlement with the association.

"There are going to be fundamental changes in our disciplinary practices growing out of the Rudman report and the Securities and Exchange Commission settlement," Barry Goldsmith, executive vice president for enforcement for NASD Regulation, Inc, said.

Under a new NASD "code of procedures" under review by SEC, disciplinary hearings will no longer be conducted by NASD district business conduct committees, said Goldsmith, speaking at a Public Securities Association conference here.
Instead, there will be a hearing panel chaired by a professional lawyer hearing officer under the new system that Goldsmith said he hopes to "get rolling" shortly after the first of the year.
Goldsmith said district conduct committees will no longer decide which enforcement cases NASD will bring. That so-called "grand jury function" will now rest with NASD in Washington
Goldsmith said NASD's hearing process will be much more formal. "If you look at SEC administrative procedures rules as a guide, all of those procedures will be incorporated," he said.
Discovery procedures, which currently vary widely among NASD districts, will be "set in stone," he said.

"You'll know what documents you can get," Goldsmith told the more than 200 securities lawyers and dealers attending the conference. He also said there will be a new practice of "formal motions" and changes in the appeals process.

NASD regulation may also provide the ability to bring temporary restraining orders and other "emergency" relief where necessary, Goldsmith said. "We need the ability to move quickly to stop certain" conduct.
Goldsmith said in worst-case scenarios, NASD will work with criminal authorities, including U.S. attorneys and local prosecutors, to bring quick action.
"The (NASD) enforcement department now is a truly national department," Goldsmith said.

Under this year's settlement with SEC, NASD agreed to allocate $100 million over the next five years to beef up its surveillance and enforcement programs. Goldsmith said NASD brought roughly 1,100 enforcement actions last year.
"We are currently running 10 to 15 percent ahead of last year," he said.
